newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli bonds end up amid dollar uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Israeli bonds end up amid dollar uncertainty.

text.p: Israeli bonds closed higher on Thursday on incread demand for CPI-linked and unlinked bonds, but prices of dollar-linked bonds continued downward, traders said.
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.07 pct to 107.47
Volume including Makams was 261 million shekels.

"Demand was up both for CPI-linked bonds and unlinked bonds. Dollar-linked bonds fell today after the dollar fell against the shekel on Wednesday," said Gidi Halpern of Meitav Investments and Securities.

The dollar regained some of its losses against the shekel on Thursday, with the representative rate for the dollar fixed at 3.5170 shekels against 3.5050 on Wednesday. However, bond prices had been influenced by the dollar's weakness in early trading on Thurday.

The soaring dollar had caused prices of unlinked bonds to fall while prices of CPI-linked short bonds rose, both on fears of higher inflation. The shekel's rebound on Tuesday and Wednesday triggered renewed demand for unlinked bonds along with continued demand for CPI-linked bonds.

"While the dollar was up people expected inflation to rise. Now, after the depreciation of the shekel has turned into an appreciation, expectations are that inflation will be up but not in a dramatic way," Halpern said.

"If before, people feared interest rates going up to curb the rise in inflation, now people expect rates to be stable," he said. "The market is still in a state of confusion about where the dollar is going."
Ilan Doron of Solid Financial Markets said demand for unlinked bonds was being generated by attractive yields.

"Yields for one-year bonds are around 12.9-13.0 percent, which is not bad considering inflation expectations of seven to eight percent," he said. "The market has calmed down and found a balance at these yield levels."
Yields on CPI-linked short bonds were 4.2 percent while on CPI-linked long bonds were around 3.95 percent, he added.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
